titulo.texto: Ceremonial Yoke with a Toad Face

frase_gancho.texto: A stone belt with a toad on the front: the game that moved the world.

puente_narrativo.texto: Yokes were fitted with pieces called palmas. Look for one shaped like a fan, with a scene of sacrifice carved into the stone.

guion_corto.texto: This U-shaped stone belt, with a toad carved on the front, measures about forty-two centimeters long. It is a yoke, one of the most characteristic images of the ballgame. On the court, players struck the rubber ball with their hips, and so they protected themselves with belts made of leather, wood, and cloth. Stone yokes were ceremonial replicas: too heavy to play in, they are thought to have been used in rituals, and some are believed to have accompanied the dead in the tomb. Look closely at the toad: the bulging eyes, the nose with open nostrils, and the bent legs, as if about to leap, which extend along the two arms of the yoke. For the peoples of the Gulf, the toad represented the damp earth and the first rains.

guion_largo.texto:
I told you we would come back to the ballgame, and here it is. The [Colossal Head](mna_s08_cabeza_colosal_6) wore a helmet that perhaps belonged to this world; the Olmec were already making rubber balls about three thousand six hundred years ago. This yoke comes from a later period, but it tells the same story: the game that, in Mesoamerica, was much more than a game.

To put it in perspective: more than a thousand ball courts have been found, from northern Mexico to Central America. No important city was without one. Two teams passed a solid rubber ball back and forth, heavy and very bouncy, and capable of causing injury. It could not be touched with the hands or the feet: it was struck with the hip, the thighs, or the forearms. Hence the belt.

But there is a curious detail. A stone yoke weighs dozens of kilos, and no one could run with one on. So what was it for? It is thought to have been a ceremonial version, made in stone to last, of the light protector that was actually worn. Something like a medal that reproduces an everyday object in metal: it is no use for work, but it celebrates it, and makes it eternal.

Now look closely at the toad. With its rough skin and its croaking, it appears when the first rains arrive, and so it came to be associated with the moisture of the earth, with fertility, and with the doorway to the underworld. Does that sound familiar? It is the same idea as [Tlaltecuhtli](mna_s06_tlaltecuhtli), the earth monster in the Mexica Hall, who was depicted with toad-like features, crouching with bent legs. Here, that animal is the guardian of the game.

And the game was not just a sport: it was a way of speaking with the cosmos. The Popol Vuh, the sacred book of the K’iche’ Maya, tells how the twins Hunahpú and Xbalanqué went down to the underworld to play ball against the lords of death, and that their fate depended on that match. Many specialists see in the game an image of the struggle between light and darkness, day and night. Each time the ball went from one side to the other, the Sun seemed to come and go with it.

One of the cities that most devoted itself to this cult was El Tajín, in this same Veracruz. It has at least seventeen ball courts, and its famous Pyramid of the Niches boasts three hundred sixty-five recesses, as many as the days of the year. The game, the calendar, and the rain appear together everywhere.

One detail recounted in the chronicles: when the Spaniards arrived, they were fascinated by the ball. They had never seen such an elastic material, and they did not understand how something could bounce like that. It is said that Hernán Cortés took a group of Mexican players to Spain, in 1528, to show them before Emperor Charles the Fifth. Imagine the scene: the ball bouncing in a European court, as if it were magic.

And the most astonishing thing is that the game did not die. In Sinaloa, to this day, people play ulama, a version that descends from that tradition: a heavy rubber ball struck with the hip. If you ever travel to Sinaloa, you will be able to watch it being played: it is one of the very few games from that world that are still alive.

texto: Look for the toad’s head, on the front, with its bulging eyes
Follow the toad’s bent legs along the two arms of the yoke
Imagine this belt on your hip: how much do you think it weighs?

texto.pregunta: Myth: Players wore these stone yokes to play.
texto.respuesta: Reality: They were ceremonial stone replicas, too heavy to play in. On the court, light protectors made of leather, wood, and cloth were used.
